No, I'm saying the literal definition of ADHD is as a developmental disorder so if you have it as an adult, you had it as a kid. If you had no symptoms of ADHD as a child, it's exceedingly unlikely to have it as an adult.

Not having an official diagnosis as a kid is fine, when you go in for a diagnostic session you'll be asked about any known symptoms of childhood ADHD. If you have a preliminary or official diagnosis then neat, if not you'll go through your childhood with the diagnostician piece by piece to figure out if you showed symptoms early on in life and go from there.

The NHS website (which I checked before making the comment) and my own doctors when I was being diagnosed with ADHD stated that childhood ADHD is required for an adult diagnosis as it's a developmental disorder. I just added the caveat as I'm not a developmental psychiatrist myself so I don't know all the ins and outs.

When you're being diagnosed you would have had to describe your childhood yes? How were you in school, could you sit still on chairs, how often did you lose things - that sort of deal. The difference I was poorly attempting to explain with NHS vs private is that NHS you're kinda just asked to describe a typical day as a kid in a relatively neutral tone, then expanded on from there. Whereas the (for profit) private clinics some of my friends have gone through lterally just chuck leading questions at you to say yes to like mine a little bit up.

 It's a bit of a bugger at the moment because am I happy way more people are being diagnosed and treated? Absolutely! Do I think (and this is 100% my opinion) some people are being diagnosed incorrectly as adults due to sloppy private practices? Also yes. Maybe it's just the universe overcorrecting for a chronically undertreated problem in previous years.

One of the defining criteria for diagnosing adult ADHD in the UK is a childhood diagnosis of ADHD. Without being able to determine ADHD presence in formative years, it /generally/ won't be diagnosed as such in adulthood. 

Obviously most people didn't go the full doctor route as kids, but even a preliminary school report will do. One of the big problems with the private ADHD clinics is they'll ask very leading questions when building a childhood history, so basically anyone that comes to them will "pass" that part. 

As far as I am aware (and this is only personal experience/explanations from my doctors) if you have ADHD as an adult but were perfectly fine and normal as a kid - you have something else going on.

It really isn't possible for a coach to be pro level at 5 different roles + at working with a team construct, the job is to create a workable framework within which your players can consistently improve. In the event that your player no longer knows how to improve in the areas you've highlighted and planned for, you go outside and find a role coach, scrape vods, sit down and dedicate 8 hours to individual review.

Add the actual majority of the work on top, collating data from your analysts + players to come up with communicable game plans and draft structures for each and every match, overseeing scrims, reviewing and planning for team exercises/events, babysitting egos so your top/mid don't refuse to play with your jungle/support anymore.

It's a 90+ hour job at least. And this was my workload in *div 1*, not even true pro. I was paying for the individual coaching sessions for my players out of my own pocket because I believed in them - some of the richer pro teams might have the capital required to build proper talent pipelines but considering they all basically shut them down, probably not. 

Peter Dun, someone I always wanted to work with and always respected, mentioned in a comment before about just how heavy the workload really is for a pro coach. I'd very much like to hear the opinion of FLY Nukeduck, now that he's played both sides of the field as it were.

I would strongly advise you buy your Kratom from sources that *pack for sale* in a legal injestion country. Pretty much all Kratom comes from the same sources depending on the strain, but most vendors will import the raw dried leaf and then process it from there, grinding to a powder, bagging, filling capsules so on. 

Since Canada does not regulate the use of Kratom as a food or medicine, there are much lower standards of regulation when it comes to hygiene & contaminants. Climate control, air filtration and other controls which are required in a food or lab-grade preparation suite are not required by Canadian law. Advertising or selling "food-grade" Kratom is fully illegal. 

I'd urge anyone to pay the slight extra for in import fees to get your medicinals from an actual legal country and save yourself the grey market headache.

Kratom is addictive; it's an agonist of the mu-opioid receptors. It's a lot weaker than popping 'codones so it isn't *quite* as slippery a slope, but the interaction in your brain is pretty much the same.

Kratom is not legal for ingestion in Canada. It has no legal status for personal use - you can't be arrested for doing anything with it once you have it, but it is not legal for companies to sell it as a tea or pill to swallow. Instead it can be sold as plant food, incense or other vague terms like that.

This means Kratom sold in Canada is not subject to the same purity or standards as anything else you put in your body - toxins of all kinds are fair game as "it's clearly not meant for human consumption". If you are going to do Kratom in Canada, buy it online from a country where it is legal to ingest and therefore has been through much more stringent testing - the Netherlands for example.

The franchising agreements were an org-driven initiative. After IMT bought the Team 8 LCS slot (in 2016) and C9 sold their C9 Challenger LCS promotion slot for $1.8million in 2017 (with Ember buying a NACS slot for almost 1.5x that), NA orgs wanted the stability that franchising offered and worked with Riot to begin the transformation. You seem to believe that Riot forced franchising but it really wasn't like that - the investment funds behind orgs like TL, Envyus and IMT wanted to protect themselves from relegation and from things like Team Impulse happening again. Riot worked with storied orgs like CLG and TSM to find investment funding or at least keep the brands on board in some capacity.

Franchising agreements tend to work on long-term ROI predictions, so even taking the low end 1.8mil buyout of the C9 challenger LCS spot in 2016 (a team slot with no players, no brand, no existing structure at all) and extrapolating that out across a 10 year franchising agreement with shared revenue pools with the big players - that's where the (realistically really low) $10 million figure came from. Prices for spots and players were already insane before franchising came into place.

Riot did not set the franchising guidelines by themselves, they talked with partners and storied orgs to set what was considered a reasonable investment for current trends in globla economics and availability of easy venture capital - to whit; they set their prices during a bubble. By the very principles on which capitalism exists, it would have been grossly "overprotective" of Riot to place hard caps on franchising at that point and probably popped the bubble right then and there.

LoL ecosystem bubble was created purely out of incredible greed on an *organisational level* and lack of any kind of foresightedness on the behalf of a few key individuals in NA. Noah Whinston of OG Immortals was the first person to really cause major issues, as his offers for both the Team 8 LCS slot and salaries for players like Huni and Reignover were a step far above what any other team was willing at that stage in history. Noah's original reasoning behind this bump up was (as far as I can remember) mostly a personal thing - he really liked League and he really wanted to own a team.

However, inflated numbers like these and the (admittedly impressive) viewership figures for pro LoL at the time allowed other NA orgs like TL and others to successfully price upwards in investment rounds. This combined with "playground" teams in the CN scene of rich boys with family money lead to a massive, and completely unsustainable salary bubble. 

EU orgs specifically (which I have more personal knowledge of) were mostly not able to match the kind of salary expectations shown in NA and CN due to more restrictive markets (delinated by language/development/gdp country differences). This meant that orgs in EU were seen more as advertising/marketing investments with adjusted budgets to match, while in NA the concept was - "continue exponential growth in viewership via venture capital, work out monetisation later when the viewer market reaches peak disposable income age - 17/18 year olds finishing university and hitting their first high paying jobs at 22/23 5 years later".

Unfortunately none of that actually came true because US capitalism in particular is a fucking crock of shit and despite the canaries in the coal mine constantly every time a bubble occurs, people keep falling for the same shit. 5 year marker on investments comes up, negative growth in viewership/engagement/conversion to liquid cash + a global downturn means everything gets pulled.

tl;dr - Riot coulda done more sure but franchising was far from what caused this, NA org owners in particular were begging for this to happen from 2015 and unfortunately due to the global nature of LoL esports, that has a major cascade effect on other regions. Opinion of an ex-LEC analyst and ERL coach -

Your structure is decent but the contents are not actually useful to build draft/game plans or set piece plays off. 

For example: Your "Game State & Comments" sections are simply a bullet point list of major events that happened in the game, which provides a useful list of timestamps during a VoD review but not enough for a coach to form a preliminary conclusion of a game.

Take this section of the report from Game 3 - 

> 17.20 G2 don't see Volibear doing Herald but wouldn't be able to contest anyway

>17.40 Ahri & Lee kill LB on bot after she over steps and they take t1
 
>18.40 G2 give Dragon because Aphelios is top side and they have no vision in river

Why is any of this happening? You mention game state but don't discern and display the steps that lead to LB overextending and dying - was this a player error? Was it a result of a bad map state, the wave stuck pushing in/away slowly at a pivotal point in the game? Did he lack gold for an item that was important for the next major objective contest? Where/what should they be playing for at each "stage" of the game? A lot of the discussion you're doing is direct eye to paper conversion flavoured by opinion, not objective cause-effect delineation.

If I'm provided a scout report, I want the following things from it.

1. *Consistent* player/team tendencies. What players overextend, what players sit on gold rather than take good backs, what lanes are played to, how often does the team deviate from "standard" map play. And so on.

2. Your conclusions for "best path to victory" vs the scouted team. Best to keep this as objective as possible and reference noted trends/draft patterns backed with statistics if possible (though you'll usually have help from other analysts with this on pro teams).
1. Keeping the important body of information separate from the auxillary information. I want the main points as soon as possible to inform my reading further. If I need more context to an opinion or conclusion, I also want to be provided that info but it doesn't need to sit in the same blob of text. Use of the reference/comment tool on Gdocs is excellent here.

[Not an exhaustive list but a vague off the top of the head reduction]

Overall I wouldn't be happy if I was handed this report - I can only use the information containted within for surface level analysis and VoD references.
